{{short description|Family of mathematical functions}}
{{Other uses|Unfolding (geometry)}}

In mathematics, an '''unfolding''' of a smooth real-valued [[function (mathematics)|function]] ''ƒ'' on a [[smooth manifold]] is a certain family of functions that includes&nbsp;''ƒ''.

== Definition ==

Let <math>M</math> be a [[smooth manifold]] and consider a smooth mapping <math> f : M \to \mathbb{R}.</math> Let us assume that for given <math> x_0 \in M</math> and <math>y_0 \in \mathbb{R}</math> we have <math> f(x_0) = y_0 </math>. Let <math> N </math> be a smooth <math>k</math>-dimensional manifold, and consider the family of mappings (parameterised by <math>N</math>) given by <math> F : M \times N \to \mathbb{R} .</math> We say that <math>F</math> is a <math>k</math>-parameter unfolding of <math>f</math> if <math>F(x,0) = f(x)</math> for all <math>x.</math> In other words the functions <math> f : M \to \mathbb{R} </math> and <math> F : M \times \{0\} \to \mathbb{R}</math> are the same: the function <math>f</math> is contained in, or is unfolded by, the family <math>F.</math>

== Example ==

Let <math> f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}</math> be given by <math>f(x,y) = x^2 + y^5.</math> An example of an unfolding of <math>f</math> would be <math> F : \mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}</math> given by 
:<math>F((x,y),(a,b,c)) = x^2 + y^5 + ay + by^2 + cy^3.</math>
As is the case with unfoldings, <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are called variables, and <math>a,</math> <math>b, </math> and <math>c</math> are called parameters, since they parameterise the unfolding.

== Well-behaved unfoldings ==

In practice we require that the unfoldings have certain properties. In <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, <math>f</math> is a smooth mapping from <math>M</math> to <math>\mathbb{R}</math> and so belongs to the [[function space]] <math>C^{\infty}(M,\mathbb{R}).</math> As we vary the parameters of the unfolding, we get different elements of the function space. Thus, the unfolding induces a function <math>\Phi : N \to C^{\infty}(M,\mathbb{R}).</math> The space <math> \operatorname{diff}(M) \times \operatorname{diff}(\mathbb{R})</math>, where <math>\operatorname{diff}(M)</math> denotes the [[group (mathematics)|group]] of [[diffeomorphism]]s of <math>M</math> etc., [[Group action (mathematics)|acts]] on <math>C^{\infty}(M,\mathbb{R}).</math> The action is given by <math>(\phi,\psi) \cdot f = \psi \circ f \circ \phi^{-1}.</math> If <math>g</math> lies in the [[group orbit|orbit]] of <math>f</math> under this action then there is a diffeomorphic change of coordinates in <math>M</math> and <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, which takes <math>g</math> to <math>f</math> (and vice versa). One property that we can impose is that 
:<math> \operatorname{Im}(\Phi) \pitchfork \operatorname{orb}(f) </math>
where "<math>\pitchfork</math>" denotes "[[Transversality (mathematics)|transverse]] to". This property ensures that as we vary the unfolding parameters we can predict – by knowing how the orbit [[foliation|foliates]] <math>C^\infty (M,\mathbb{R})</math> – how the resulting functions will vary.

== Versal unfoldings ==

There is an idea of a versal unfolding. Every versal unfolding has the property that 
<math> \operatorname{Im}(\Phi) \pitchfork \operatorname{orb}(f) </math>, but the converse is false. Let <math>x_1,\ldots,x_n</math> be [[local coordinates]] on <math>M</math>, and let <math>\mathcal{O}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> denote the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] of smooth functions. We define the [[Jacobian ideal]] of <math>f</math>, denoted by <math>J_f</math>, as follows:

:<math> J_f := \left\langle \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \ldots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \right\rangle. </math>

Then a [[basis (mathematics)|basis]] for a versal unfolding of <math>f</math> is given by the [[quotient ring|quotient]]

:<math> \frac{\mathcal{O}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)}{J_f}</math>.

This quotient is known as the local algebra of <math>f</math>. The dimension of the local algebra is called the [[Milnor number]] of <math>f</math>. The minimum number of unfolding parameters for a versal unfolding is equal to the Milnor number; that is not to say that every unfolding with that many parameters will be versal. Consider the function <math>f(x,y) = x^2 + y^5</math>. A calculation shows that

:<math> \frac{\mathcal{O}(x,y)}{\langle 2x, 5y^4 \rangle} = \{y,y^2,y^3\} \ . </math>

This means that <math>\{y,y^2,y^3\}</math> give a basis for a versal unfolding, and that 

:<math>F((x,y),(a,b,c)) = x^2 + y^5 + ay + by^2 + cy^3</math>

is a versal unfolding. A versal unfolding with the minimum possible number of unfolding parameters is called a miniversal unfolding.

== Bifurcations sets of unfoldings ==

An important object associated to an unfolding is its bifurcation set. This set lives in the [[parameter space]] of the unfolding, and gives all parameter values for which the resulting function has degenerate singularities.

== Other terminology ==

Sometimes unfoldings are called deformations, versal unfoldings are called versal deformations, etc.
